JSON: Name: chp_a2a_hydrocephalus_pipeline Title: AAV-mediated choroid plexus targeting and pharmacological antagonism of adenosine A2A receptor signaling to reduce CSF hypersecretion and ventriculomegaly in hydrocephalus Short Hypothesis: Selective inhibition of adenosine A2A receptor signaling in choroid plexus epithelial cells causally reduces CSF production and prevents ventriculomegaly in rodent models of hydrocephalus. Related Work: Prior studies have identified the choroid plexus as a major site of CSF production and implicated transporters and channels (e.g., NKCC1, SPAK, AQP1, Na+-K+-ATPase isoforms) in CSF secretion. Pharmacological inhibitors of NKCC1 and systemically delivered diuretics have shown limited and inconsistent benefit due to poor CNS selectivity and peripheral side effects. Work linking inflammation/hemorrhage to CSF hypersecretion has pointed to toll-like receptor signaling and cytokine cascades, but a direct molecular mediator between elevated extracellular signals and altered choroid plexus ion transport has not been established. Cell-type nonselective approaches and systemic inhibitors lack spatial precision required to disentangle choroid-plexus-specific mechanisms, and prior interventions have not demonstrated pathway-level causality (necessity and sufficiency) linking a discrete receptor to downstream SPAK phosphorylation and ATP1A2 regulation. Translation is further limited by insufficient demonstration of efficacy across hemorrhagic and obstructive hydrocephalus models and by the instability of extracellular nucleoside measurements in clinical samples. Abstract: Hydrocephalus from hemorrhage, infection, or trauma is frequently driven by choroid plexus-mediated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) hypersecretion, yet mechanistic links and effective pharmacotherapies are lacking. We propose a structured pipeline that tests whether targeted inhibition of adenosine A2A receptor signaling in choroid plexus epithelial cells reduces CSF production and ventricular enlargement. The approach integrates cell-specific genetic perturbation using AAV-delivered constructs, pharmacological A2A antagonism, and pathway-level manipulations (SPAK knockdown, ATP1A2 overexpression) across two rodent hydrocephalus models and human CSF profiling. Primary readouts include CSF adenosine concentration, MRI-based ventricle volume, quantitative CSF production, and molecular endpoints (p-SPAK, ATP1A2). The main contribution is a preclinical, mechanistic evaluation that establishes necessity and sufficiency of choroid-plexus A2A→PI3K/Akt→p-SPAK and A2A→NF-κB→ATP1A2 axes in CSF hypersecretion. Expected outcomes are: (1) demonstration that ChP-selective A2A inhibition reduces CSF output and ventriculomegaly, and (2) identification of pathway biomarkers for translational pharmacological targeting. Experiments: Datasets and models: (1) Human CSF samples: archived lumbar/cisternal CSF from hydrocephalus patients (n=11) and neurologic control subjects (n=8) for adenosine quantification by UPLC. (2) Rodent cohorts: adult C57BL/6 mice randomized into experimental groups. Hydrocephalus induction: (A) post-hemorrhagic model via intracerebroventricular autologous blood injection; (B) obstructive model via intraventricular kaolin. Genetic/pharmacological interventions: AAV2/5-mediated ChP-targeted constructs: A2A-OE, A2A-shRNA (A2A-Kd), SPAK-shRNA (SPAK-Kd), ATP1A2-OE, and scramble/control AAV. Pharmacology: systemic KW6002 (istradefylline) vs vehicle; PI3K inhibitor GDC-0941, Akt inhibitor MK-2206, NF-κB inhibitor JSH-23 for pathway interrogation in vitro. Grouping and sample sizes: n=8–12 mice per group; groups include: sham+scramble, PHH+scramble, PHH+A2A-Kd, PHH+KW6002, PHH+A2A-OE, PHH+A2A-OE+SPAK-Kd, PHH+A2A-OE+ATP1A2-OE; analogous groups for kaolin model. Timepoints: baseline, day 5 and day 14 post-induction. Primary endpoints and metrics: (1) Ventricle volume by high-field MRI and manual segmentation (mm3); (2) CSF production rate via cisterna magna collection (μL/min); (3) CSF adenosine concentration by validated UPLC (μM); (4) molecular assays: p-SPAK/total SPAK and ATP1A2 protein levels by quantitative western blot densitometry and immunofluorescence (normalized to housekeeping protein and ROI-corrected fluorescence intensity); (5) tracer-based CSF flow (Evans blue distribution) scored qualitatively and quantified by spectrophotometry of microdissected regions; (6) behavioral and survival measures if applicable. Baselines and comparators: scramble AAV and vehicle treatments; comparison to SPAK-Kd and ATP1A2-OE provides mechanistic ablations testing necessity and sufficiency of downstream nodes. In vitro assays: primary ChP epithelial cells transduced with A2A-OE or control, treated with PI3K/Akt/NF-κB inhibitors; endpoints p-SPAK and ATP1A2 protein-level changes measured by western blot; n=4 biological replicates per condition. Statistical analysis: sample size justification to detect effect size d≥1.0 with power≥0.8; data tested for normality; ANOVA with post-hoc Tukey for multi-group comparisons or Mann–Whitney U for non-normal pairwise tests; significance threshold p<0.05. Ablation studies: (i) SPAK-Kd in A2A-OE mice to test whether SPAK is necessary for A2A-driven CSF hypersecretion; (ii) ATP1A2-OE in A2A-OE mice to test whether restoring ATP1A2 is sufficient to rescue CSF overproduction. Secondary comparisons: KW6002 vs A2A-Kd to compare pharmacologic vs genetic efficacy; PI3K/Akt/NF-κB inhibition in vitro to map pathway dependencies. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: incomplete or uneven AAV2/5 transduction of choroid plexus epithelium, off-target transduction in adjacent brain regions, immune responses to viral vectors, and instability/degradation of adenosine in collected CSF leading to measurement artifacts. Biological compensation: redundancy among adenosine receptor subtypes or parallel inflammatory pathways may attenuate effect size; chronic receptor blockade may induce receptor up- or down-regulation altering long-term outcomes. Model limitations: rodent PHH and kaolin models may not fully recapitulate human hydrocephalus etiologies and chronicity; efficacy in non-obstructive versus obstructive forms may differ. Evaluation and data biases: small clinical CSF sample sizes and clinical heterogeneity (age, etiology, prior treatments) reduce external validity; CSF sampling location and timing introduce variability. Scalability and translational constraints: AAV-mediated ChP-specific gene therapy faces delivery, safety, and regulatory hurdles for human translation; systemic KW6002 effects on peripheral tissues and on CNS clearance mechanisms may cause off-target outcomes. Resource constraints: high-field MRI throughput and UPLC assay capacity limit sample processing rate. Generalization limits: findings establishing A2A→SPAK/ATP1A2 axis in mice may not generalize across species, developmental stages, or comorbid conditions.
